headline: This law directs more money into the Crime Victims Fund and changes how states get victim compensation and assistance grants.
what_it_does: The law sends money from deferred prosecution and non-prosecution agreements into the Crime Victims Fund instead of the general Treasury fund. It raises the share of state victim compensation payments used to calculate federal formula grants from 60% to 75%. It also lets states waive the matching-funds requirement for victim assistance grants during and for one year after a pandemic-related national emergency, and allows states to waive it under their own policies.

who_it_affects.group: Crime victims who apply to state compensation programs
who_it_affects.how: Because the formula base is larger, states may receive more federal grant money to pay compensation to victims of crime.
These programs can use a higher share of their prior-year payments to calculate federal formula grants.

who_it_affects.group: State victim assistance programs and their grant recipients
who_it_affects.how: They may be excused from providing matching funds during a pandemic-related emergency and for one year afterward, or under a state-established policy.

who_it_affects.group: Companies and organizations that enter deferred prosecution or non-prosecution agreements with the government
who_it_affects.how: Money paid under these agreements is now deposited into the Crime Victims Fund rather than the general Treasury fund.

when_it_takes_effect: The law was enacted on July 22, 2021, and its changes took effect on that date.
